summary.text: For every prime \(p\), the only admissible integers up to \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)=2\). Taking \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and an arbitrarily large prime \(p\ge 60\) gives \(\log p>4\), hence \((\log p)^{1/2}>2=a(p)\), contradicting the proposed eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime divisor of }k\text{ divides }n\}.
\]
Thus the condition on \(k\) says that the set of prime factors of \(k\) is a subset of the set of prime factors of \(n\). We will show that the proposed assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n)
\tag{1}
\]
is false. Here \(\log\) is the natural logarithm, and the power is the usual real power.

The key observation is that \(a(n)\) stays as small as possible along the infinite sequence of prime numbers.

**Lemma.** If \(p\) is prime, then \(a(p)=2\).

Indeed, the set of prime factors of \(p\) is the singleton \(\{p\}\). Certainly \(k=1\) is counted by \(a(p)\), because \(1\) has no prime factors, and \(k=p\) is counted because its only prime factor is \(p\).

Conversely, suppose that \(1\le k\le p\) and every prime factor of \(k\) lies in \(\{p\}\). If \(k=1\), this is one of the two values already listed. If \(k\ne1\), then \(k>1\), so \(k\) has a prime divisor \(q\). By the assumed containment of prime-factor sets, \(q=p\). Hence \(p\mid k\). Since \(k>0\), divisibility gives \(p\le k\), while by hypothesis \(k\le p\). Thus \(k=p\). Therefore the only counted integers are \(1\) and \(p\), proving
\[
a(p)=2.
\tag{2}
\]

We also record a concrete logarithmic estimate that will be used below:
\[
4<\log p\qquad\text{whenever }p\ge60.
\tag{3}
\]
To justify it, first note that
\[
e=\exp(1)<2.7182818286.
\tag{4}
\]
For completeness, this decimal inequality can be obtained directly from the exponential series. Truncate after the term \(1/11!\). For every \(j\ge1\),
\[
(11+j)!=11!\,(12)(13)\cdots(11+j)\ge 11!\,12^j.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
e
&=\sum_{r=0}^{11}\frac1{r!}+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac1{(11+j)!}\\
&\le \sum_{r=0}^{11}\frac1{r!}
  +\frac1{11!}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac1{12^j}\\
&=\sum_{r=0}^{11}\frac1{r!}+\frac1{11!\,11}
 <2.7182818286.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last inequality is exact rational arithmetic; the difference between \(2.7182818286\) and the displayed rational upper bound is
\[
\frac{42551}{343035000000000}>0.
\]
Raising (4) to the fourth power, which preserves the strict inequality because both sides are positive, gives
\[
\exp(4)=\exp(1)^4<(2.7182818286)^4<55.
\tag{5}
\]
The final comparison is again rational arithmetic: in fact
\[
(2.7182818286)^4
=
\frac{34123843777793029748544875305108782813601}
{625000000000000000000000000000000000000}
<55.
\]
Thus, if \(p\ge60\), then
\[
\exp(4)<55<60\le p.
\]
Since the natural logarithm is the increasing inverse of the exponential function on positive real numbers, this implies \(4<\log p\), establishing (3).

We now disprove (1). Suppose, for contradiction, that (1) holds. Apply it with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There would then be a natural number \(N\) such that every natural number \(n\ge N\) satisfies
\[
(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\tag{6}
\]

Choose a prime number
\[
p\ge \max\{N,60\}.
\tag{7}
\]
Such a prime exists by Euclid's theorem that there are primes above every bound. One may see the precise form needed here as follows: for a given bound \(B\), take a prime divisor \(p\) of \(B!+1\). If \(p<B\), or more generally if \(p\le B\), then \(p\mid B!\), while also \(p\mid B!+1\), forcing \(p\mid1\), which is impossible. Hence a prime above the prescribed bound exists. Applying this to a bound at least \(\max\{N,60\}\) yields (7) (and the usual infinitude-of-primes formulation directly gives a prime greater than or equal to that maximum).

Because \(p\ge N\), inequality (6) applies to \(p\). By the lemma,
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)=2.
\tag{8}
\]
On the other hand, \(p\ge60\), so (3) gives \(\log p>4\). Both bases are positive, and the function \(x\mapsto x^{1/2}\) is strictly increasing on the positive reals. Therefore
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}>4^{1/2}=2.
\tag{9}
\]
Inequalities (8) and (9) contradict one another.

Thus no threshold \(N\) can make the claimed lower bound hold even for the single choice \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\). Hence the conjecture that, for every \(\epsilon>0\), one has
\[
a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\) is false.
